summary: Establishes an IETF URN sub-namespace for use with OAuth-related specifications. This gives them a place for stable, unique names. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

eli5.summary: OAuth things need unique names, like labels on lunchboxes. This memo makes a special label area just for OAuth so names never clash.

questions: where do oauth urns come from
how to register an oauth urn
what is the oauth uri registry
subtitle: A reserved place in the URN space where OAuth specifications can register stable names.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 extensions use URIs to identify themselves, and they need a shared, collision-free place to get those names.
tldr.mechanism: It registers the IETF URN sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:oauth and creates an IANA registry under it, with a template and Specification Required as the procedure.
tldr.outcome: OAuth-related URNs can now be registered in the form urn:ietf:params:oauth followed by a colon and a value.

today: RFC 6755 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It still defines the urn:ietf:params:oauth sub-namespace and how to register under it.

sections.title: Why an OAuth URN Space
sections.content: Extensions and companion specifications to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework use URIs to identify the extension in use or other context. This document creates and registers an IETF URN sub-namespace, as RFC 3553 allows, for such specifications. The new sub-namespace is urn:ietf:params:oauth, and OAuth parameters are established beneath it.
sections.eli5: OAuth gets its own shelf in a huge name library, so its names stay together and never clash.

sections.title: How to Register a Name
sections.content:
A registrant requests a URN of the form urn:ietf:params:oauth:<value>, where the value represents the functionality being registered. The procedure is Specification Required under RFC 5226, and the request uses a template with these fields:

  • URN: the URI that identifies the functionality.
  • Common Name: the name by which it is generally known.
  • Change Controller: state IETF for Standards Track RFCs, otherwise the responsible party.
  • Specification Document(s): a reference to the document defining it.
sections.eli5: To get a name, you fill in a short form saying what it is, what people call it, who is in charge and where it is written down.

sections.title: An Example Request
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example request for a new OAuth 2.0 grant type: URN urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:example, Common Name "An Example Grant Type for OAuth 2.0", Change controller IETF.

It suggests that the value include a class and an identifier-within-class separated by a colon, though other compositions may be used.
sections.eli5: The example is a filled-in form for a pretend new kind of OAuth permission.

sections.title: IANA Actions and Security
sections.content:
IANA has registered the sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:oauth per RFC 3553. It also created an "OAuth URI" registry for URNs under it, placed in a new top-level registry called "OAuth Parameters".

There are no additional security considerations beyond those inherent to using URNs (RFC 2141), though anyone working on OAuth is advised to know the security considerations of OAuth 2.0.
sections.eli5: The librarians made the new shelf and a sign-in book for it. There is no special danger beyond what names already have.

references.text: Mealling, M., et al., "An IETF URN Sub-namespace for Registered Protocol Parameters", BCP 73, RFC 3553, June 2003.
Narten, T. and H. Alvestrand, "Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs", BCP 26, RFC 5226, May 2008.
